results.label: 6A
results.summary: Ranges are now widened by one factor per quantity and horizon, set against the truth on four earlier synthetic worlds, which works there but on this world puts only 9 of 18 quantities between 85/100 and 95/100 on Forecasts against later estimates (6 before). Capacity rises from 74 to 83, but the overall rate falls from 94 to 87, and overdue orders, lost demand and utilization drop to 70-80 because this world revises them far more than the earlier worlds did.

results.label: 10B
results.summary: What the data pin down now gives a second, stricter figure for every sector, comparing each parameter's uncertainty with what its group's average alone would give rather than with the starting guess. By that measure 58% of entity parameters are informed by data, not 91%, and the input-cost pass-through and normal markup are learned for only about one entity in ten.

results.label: 3A
results.summary: Letting the filter adjust each entity's order level in Housing, Retail, Data centers, Machinery and Airlines lowered the new-orders spread ratio almost everywhere, but only Airlines reached 1; Housing (5.3), Data centers (2.3), Retail (1.9) and Machinery (1.8) still grow less certain about new orders when data are added. The true nowcast error improved (whole world 0.0469 to 0.0445, the five sectors 0.0433 to 0.0338), though the filter change alone did as well as the change with refitting, and Retail's lost demand became unsettled (0.86 to 3.31).

results.label: 1A
results.summary: Giving Wholesale an official monthly price index cut its gap on Forecasts against later estimates from 12.4% to 4.1% and raised its hit rate from 76/100 to 91/100; used instead as a sector price observation it gave 5.5% and 90/100. Wholesale's true nowcast error fell from 6.7% to about 5.8%, but used only as an official statistic the index conflicts with Wholesale's other data, so the next step is to use it in fitting as well.

results.label: 9C
results.summary: Adding advance-booking observations for Hotels and Airlines and signed-not-started leases for Data centers met the check only for the Data centers order book (spread ratio 0.88 to 0.74); Hotels' order book (0.88) and lead time in both sectors (about 0.93 and 1.00) stayed set mostly by the model. Accuracy against the truth improved clearly where the data were added: Hotels' error halved (0.051 to 0.026) and Airlines' order-book error fell from 0.025 to 0.013, though part of the whole-world gain (0.0469 to 0.0409) is run-to-run noise.

results.label: 7A
results.summary: Comparing sector totals with official statistics now allows for the statistic's own uncertainty, which raises the share of months inside the range from 82/100 to 92/100: Hotels employees go from 51 to 95, Hospitals employees from 62 to 100, Food utilization from 75 to 91 and Chemicals utilization from 74 to 84. Machinery production, 5.8% off, still clearly disagrees (1/100), though 9 of the 22 statistics now sit at 98-100, so the range may be a little wide.

results.label: 9A
results.summary: Data centers' overdue orders and phantom orders, which never vary, now show as fixed by the model's structure instead of a spread ratio of 1.00, so the count of quantities that come mostly from the model falls from 49 to 47. Lead time stays as it was, correctly: its copies do differ (ratio 0.999), so it really does come mostly from the model.

results.label: 10A
results.summary: Sharing capacity drift, emissions slope and list-price gap across each sector's entities, chosen sector by sector on withheld observations, was kept in 6 of 9 sectors, and the share of informative parameters would rise from about 91% to 93% only because weakly learned rows drop out. In those 6 sectors the true nowcast error got worse (4.8% to 5.2%, with Retail 7.0% to 9.1% and Machinery 5.5% to 8.0%); the whole-world improvement (4.7% to 4.1%) came from Semiconductors, which the change did not touch, so it is run-to-run noise.

results.label: 2A
results.summary: Anchoring the size of Machinery's untracked firms to the official production statistic brought Machinery production from 0/100 to 100/100 on Sector totals against official statistics (gap 5.2% to 0.8%), utilization from 58 to 99, and the page's overall rate from 82 to 89, while sharply cutting Machinery's true output, shipments and new-orders errors on both seeds. The cost is Machinery's finished stock, which nothing observes: it went badly wrong at one run date on seed20261112, leaving Machinery's overall true error about flat there (5.5% to 5.7%) while it fell on seed20261107 (4.4% to 2.9%).

results.label: 3B
results.summary: Adding direct new-orders statistics for Machinery, Semiconductors, Housing and Data centers did not bring new orders' spread ratio below 0.8 in any of them (2.0, 1.2, 5.2 and 2.9 afterwards), even though the model fits the new readings well. Machinery and Housing got less accurate against the truth while the whole-world gain (0.0469 to 0.0439) came mostly from Semiconductors, which suggests the spread ratio itself may be the wrong measure for new orders.

results.label: 8A
results.summary: Adding monthly sector materials inventories for six manufacturing sectors, and company raw-material reports for oil and gas and homebuilders, pinned input inventory in Food, Chemicals, Steel and Autos (spread ratios 0.18-0.76, from about 1) and cut its true nowcast error from 0.032 to 0.021. But other quantities in those sectors got worse, Machinery, Semiconductors, Housing and Oil and gas stayed above 0.8, and Oil and gas's 2023 fit blew up, so the overall true error worsened (0.0454 to 0.0504 leaving that one fit out).

results.label: 4A
results.summary: Measuring the spread ratio from total spread over the history removes most of the very large values (quantities above 1.2 fall from 13-18 per date to 7-13) and identifies the runaway copies behind several of them, such as Hospitals' and Hotels' lost demand. Retail does not fall toward 1: its order book, new orders, shipments and load factor stay at 2.8-3.5 with no runaway copies, so the data really do spread Retail's copies about three times wider, which points at the filter's updates there rather than the measure.

results.label: 5A
results.summary: Giving every kind of business a small monthly capacity revision raised Capacity on Forecasts against later estimates from 74/100 to 95/100 and shrank its gap (0.018 to 0.013), with large gains in Housing, Food and Hotels, and true nowcast error fell from 0.0469 to 0.0417. But it also widened other ranges (overall hit rate 94 to 98) and overshoots the 90 target for capacity, so a smaller revision is the next thing to try; Wholesale's capacity did not improve.

results.label: 9B
results.summary: Letting the filter adjust the order level of Hotels, Hospitals and Data centers cut their shipments and order-book spread ratios from about 0.9 to 0.4-0.75 on both seeds, but lead time did not move and the ranges with data did not actually narrow: the ratios fell mainly because the model without data now carries more uncertainty. The true nowcast error improved a little (whole world 0.0469 to 0.0458 and 0.0445 on two seeds; Hotels 0.0505 to 0.0342 and 0.0465).

results.label: 5B
results.summary: Capacity now gets its own widening factor, set on three earlier synthetic worlds, which raises its hit rate on Forecasts against later estimates from 74/100 to 86/100, short of the 90/100 target. Its true-value coverage rises from about 0.77 to 0.84 with no change in error; the factor needed varies a lot from world to world, and capacity's misses look like level shifts that wider ranges alone will not fix.

results.label: 6B
results.summary: Forecasts against later estimates now leaves out the 1,812 of 6,408 values whose later estimate comes mostly from the model, which moves the overall hit rate from 94/100 to 93/100 and the typical gap from 2.5% to 2.2%. The stated cause holds only for input inventory: lead time, order book and announced capacity still score 100/100 on data-informed values alone, so those ranges are simply too wide.

results.label: 2B
results.summary: Letting the filter adjust Machinery's order level and overdue orders month by month raised its Observations against the model from 85/100 to 96/100, its agreement with official production from 0/100 (5.8% off) to 73/100 (1.9% off) and with official utilization from 54 to 99, and cut its true nowcast error from 0.055 to 0.035. A second run on other random numbers improved the same way but much less on official production (13/100), so fit-to-fit noise is still large, and Machinery's ranges now look wider than they need to be.
